title: Visual Instruction Tuning Aligns Modalities through Abstraction
claim: Image and text inputs, though encoded differently, converge in a shared abstraction stage of the model's middle layers, which is the only part that needs adapting.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right; two input rows converge on a highlighted middle block
description: A left-to-right flow diagram with two input rows. The top row starts with a red panda photo and the question "What animal is this?". The image passes through a pink ViT box and a pink Connector box. The text passes through a green Tokenizer box. The bottom row starts with a caption describing the same animal, plus the same question, and goes through a green Tokenizer. Both rows enter blue "Early layers" blocks marked with snowflakes for frozen. Curved arrows from both rows meet in a large orange "Intermediate layers" column. That column holds a circle labelled "Shared abstraction" with a red panda icon and the words "Red Panda", and a fire icon for trained. The flow then goes to a frozen blue "Late layers" block and the output "Red Panda". Numbered headers label three phases: unimodal processing, abstraction and generation. The orange middle column draws the eye first.
caption: Visual and textual abstractions align in the intermediate layers of VLMs. \looseness=-1We compare two semantically equivalent inputs: (1) a multimodal prompt, where an image is encoded and injected into the LLM through a visual connector, and (2) a text-only prompt, where the image is replaced by a natural-language caption describing the same content. For both inputs, we track the hidden representation of the final contextualized input token across the layers of the LLM. The backbone can be divided into three functional regions: early layers that process modality-specific information, intermediate layers that form shared semantic abstractions, and late layers that specialize in answer generation. Our results show that visual instruction tuning primarily aligns image-derived representations with pre-existing textual abstractions in the intermediate layers. Moreover, fine-tuning only this region is sufficient to recover nearly the full performance of standard vision-language fine-tuning.
abstract: Visual instruction tuning effectively adapts a pre-trained Large Language Model (LLM) to process image information alongside text. Yet it remains unclear how visual features are embedded within the layer-wise hierarchy of abstractions in the LLM backbone. Across a diverse set of vision-language architectures, we show that instruction tuning primarily serves as a bridge, embedding visual features directly into the intermediate semantic layers of the LLM, bypassing the early layers devoted to unimodal processing. With probing analyses and causal interventions, we show that these intermediate layers constitute the semantic core of vision-language processing and play a critical role in performance across a broad set of multimodal benchmarks. In addition, by comparing the geometry of semantically equivalent visual and textual representations, we find that fine-tuning extends and strengthens the existing abstraction phase, aligning visual features with pre-existing textual ones. Finally, we confirm the functional role of this localized alignment by restricting fine-tuning to intermediate layers alone: this strategy preserves the performance of full fine-tuning on vision-centric benchmarks while reducing training time. Our results suggest that multimodal integration is a localized phenomenon driven by the repurposing of the internal abstraction engine of the LLM.
